say: You give it a polynomial with real coefficients and one complex root. It finds **all** the roots.
The key idea: complex roots of a real polynomial come in **conjugate** pairs, so $a+bi$ being a root forces $a-bi$ to be one too.

how.higher: On Higher Paper 1 it is a step inside a bigger complex-number question: 2016 Q1(c) (a quadratic with a complex coefficient) and 2019 Q5(a) (finding $p$ and $q$), each worth 10 marks.

example.question: $2 + i$ is a root of $z^3 - 6z^2 + 13z - 10 = 0$, where $z \in \mathbb{C}$. Find the other two roots.

steps.title: Write down the conjugate
steps.say: The coefficients are all real, so complex roots come in conjugate pairs. The root $\hl{1}{2+i}$ forces the root $\hl{2}{2-i}$.

steps.title: Build the quadratic factor
steps.say: Multiply the two linear factors. The imaginary parts cancel in the sum, and the product of a number and its conjugate is real.

steps.title: Divide to find the last factor
steps.say: The cubic is the quadratic times a linear factor $(z+c)$. The leading term gives $z$, and the constant term $-10$ must equal $5c$, so $c=-2$.

lines.text: Multiply out to check: you get the cubic back.

steps.title: Read off the third root
steps.say: The last factor is zero when $z = 2$.

higher.tip: Write the conjugate root down straight away. Identifying the second root earns marks by itself.
Use the sum and the product of the two roots to form the quadratic. Formulating them as equations earns high partial credit.
If you divide, set the long division up correctly and get the first two lines right. That is where the partial credit is.

say: You give it an equation $z^n = a$. It finds all $n$ roots, in polar and rectangular form.
The key idea: write $a$ in polar form, take the $n$th root of the modulus, and **divide the angle by $n$**. The roots sit on a circle, evenly spaced $\frac{2\pi}{n}$ apart.

how.higher: On Higher Paper 1 it is a part of its own, worth 10 marks in 2019 and 2021 and 15 marks in 2023 and 2025. Polar form is required to earn any credit.

example.question: Solve $z^4 = -16$, giving your answers in the form $a + bi$.

steps.title: Write $-16$ in polar form
steps.say: The number $-16$ lies on the negative real axis. Its modulus is $\hl{1}{16}$ and its angle is $\hl{2}{\pi}$. Add $2n\pi$ so that every angle is covered.

steps.title: Take the fourth root
steps.say: De Moivre: raise the modulus to the power $\frac14$ and multiply the angle by $\frac14$.

steps.title: Find two roots
steps.say: Put $n=0$ and $n=1$ and write each in the form $a+bi$.

steps.title: Use symmetry for the rest
steps.say: The roots are evenly spaced around a circle, so the other two are the negatives of these.

higher.tip: Work in polar form. Without it you earn nothing, even if the roots come out right.

say: You give it $\cos n\theta$ or $\sin n\theta$. It writes it as an identity in powers of $\cos\theta$ or $\sin\theta$.
The key idea: expand $(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^n$ with the binomial theorem, and **equate real parts** (for cosine) or imaginary parts (for sine) with De Moivre's $\cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta$.

how.higher: On Higher Paper 1 it was a 10 mark part of 2025 Q4(b), where the student equated real parts to get a double-angle identity.

example.question: Use De Moivre's Theorem to show that $\cos 4\theta = 8\cos^4\theta - 8\cos^2\theta + 1$.

steps.title: Apply De Moivre
steps.say: De Moivre says the fourth power of $\cos\theta + i\sin\theta$ is found by multiplying the angle by 4. Its real part is $\hl{1}{\cos 4\theta}$.

steps.title: Expand with the binomial theorem
steps.say: Expand the same bracket the long way. Use $i^2=-1$, $i^3=-i$ and $i^4=1$.

steps.title: Equate real parts
steps.say: The two expansions are equal, so their real parts are equal. Pick out the terms without $i$.

steps.title: Remove the sines
steps.say: The target has only cosines. Replace $\sin^2\theta$ with $1-\cos^2\theta$, then simplify.

higher.tip: After expanding, equate the real parts with the real parts. That is the step that gives the identity.
Writing the bracket out as a product, or starting the expansion, is work of merit and earns low partial credit.

say: You give it the statement $(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^n = \cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta$ for whole numbers $n$. It proves it by induction.
The key idea: assume it for $n=k$, multiply by one more $(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)$, and the **compound angle formulae** turn the product into the $n=k+1$ case.

how.higher: On Higher Paper 1 it was 2018 Q4(a), worth 15 marks, with credit for each step of the induction.

example.question: Prove by induction that $[r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)]^n = r^n(\cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta)$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

steps.title: Test $n=1$
steps.say: Put $n=1$ into both sides. They match.

steps.title: Assume $n=k$
steps.say: Suppose the statement is true for $n=k$. This is the one fact we are allowed to use.

steps.title: Prove it for $n=k+1$
steps.say: Write the power $k+1$ as the power $k$ times one more bracket. Replace the power $k$ with the assumption, then multiply out. $i^2=-1$.

lines.tex: &= r^k(\cos k\theta + i\sin k\theta) \cdot r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)
&= r^{k+1}\big[(\cos k\theta\cos\theta - \sin k\theta\sin\theta) + i(\sin k\theta\cos\theta + \cos k\theta\sin\theta)\big]

lines.text: The two brackets are the compound angle formulae for $\cos(A+B)$ and $\sin(A+B)$.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.say: Say what has been shown, in words. The marks are tied to the conclusion.

lines.text: True for $n=1$. If true for $n=k$ then true for $n=k+1$. Therefore true for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

higher.tip: End with a conclusion in words. Leaving it out costs a mark on an otherwise correct proof.
The steps for $n=1$, $n=k$ and $n=k+1$ can come in any order, and each earns partial credit.
The full $r$ version, proved correctly, earns full credit.
